title: Induction as the basis of recursion correctness

claims.text: Floyd’s method imposes a condition on each command guaranteeing that whenever a command is reached by a connection whose proposition is true, it will be left, if at all, by a connection whose proposition is true. The conclusion about the whole program then follows by induction on the number of commands executed.

source.title: Floyd, R. W., Assigning Meanings to Programs, Proceedings of Symposia in Applied Mathematics 19:19-32, American Mathematical Society, 1967

claims.text: Floyd states the aim as establishing a rigorous standard for proofs about programs, including proofs of correctness, equivalence and termination — termination being treated separately from the rest.

source.title: Floyd, R. W., Assigning Meanings to Programs, Proceedings of Symposia in Applied Mathematics 19:19-32, American Mathematical Society, 1967

claims.text: Hoare’s notation asserts that if the precondition holds before the program runs, the postcondition holds when it ends. It offers no guarantee of termination, since execution from a state satisfying the precondition need not halt.

source.title: Hoare, C. A. R., An Axiomatic Basis for Computer Programming, Communications of the ACM 12(10):576-580, 1969

beats.broke: a recursive function calls itself, so any attempt to justify it by tracing the execution never bottoms out
beats.fix: assume the function is correct on smaller inputs, prove it correct on this one, and check the base case — which is induction with the names changed
beats.cost: the argument establishes that the answer is right if one is produced, and says nothing about whether the recursion stops
beats.interview: why assuming the function already works is not circular reasoning
